Adipose tissue inflammation

One mouse experiment found nearly fivefold smaller abdominal adipose inflammatory areas and lower blood glucose 24 hours after the final PBM session. No human evidence was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One mouse experiment found nearly fivefold smaller abdominal adipose inflammatory areas and lower blood glucose 24 hours after the final PBM session. No human evidence was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

One 2016 publication directly examined adipose-tissue inflammation in male mice with diet-induced obesity and hyperglycemia. The report combines tissue histology with a short-term glucose measurement. No exact-category human study or separate cell-culture experiment was identified. Adjacent PBM studies of glucose metabolism or cultured adipocytes address related biology but are not counted as direct evidence for adipose inflammatory infiltration.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study has tested PBM for adipose-tissue inflammation in people. The mouse measurements therefore cannot establish effects on human body fat, diabetes control, or inflammatory disease.

Animal evidence

In the experiment, untreated obese mice had abdominal adipose inflammatory areas almost five times larger than those in the irradiated group. Blood glucose was also lower in treated mice 24 hours after the last session. The tissue difference directly supports reduced inflammatory infiltration in this model. The glucose result is a short-term association; the study did not show that reduced fat inflammation caused it or that glycemic control persisted (Yoshimura et al. 2016).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo experiment on PBM treatment of inflamed adipose tissue was identified in this indication category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used an 843-nm near-infrared LED at 60 mW, 0.019 W/cm² and 5.7 J/cm². Each exposure lasted 300 seconds, with six sessions across three weeks. Light was delivered over the abdominal region of the mice. The experiment did not compare wavelengths or doses, and its body-surface exposure does not establish how light would reach human adipose tissue at different depths.

Interpretation

The treated mice had smaller abdominal fat inflammatory areas, and their glucose was lower at the single 24-hour measurement. These are favorable findings within one short animal experiment. They do not yet show a durable metabolic effect or establish that PBM reduces adipose inflammation in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reduced adipose inflammation and short-term glucose levels in obese mice
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One mouse experiment found substantially smaller inflammatory areas in abdominal fat and lower blood glucose shortly after the final treatment. These findings are direct for the animal model, but have not been independently replicated and do not establish a lasting metabolic effect in people. Replication with longer follow-up and human studies measuring adipose and metabolic outcomes would strengthen the evidence.
